extracted.intended_audience: scientists and academic researchers who apply for grants (especially NIH applicants) and those interested in grant-funded research careers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for NIH grant applicants on whether and how to take concerns about their assigned Program Officer up the chain (other POs, Branch Chief, Division Director), plus related career-and-funding advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'escalate' in an entitled/angry way
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ok, first of all ‘escalate’ is the wrong way to think about it. So don’t do that.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are unhappy with your assigned PO, avoid framing contact as an escalation or as entitled complaining; angry demands about bias or incompetence are counterproductive. Maintain composure and do not attack the PO personally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore opinions/input of other Program Officers
rubrics_metrics.description: “You should absolutely explore the opinions and input of other Program Officers if you are unhappy with the responses (or lack thereof) that you are getting from your assigned PO.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit perspectives from other POs (peers within the IC) as an alternative to direct confrontation. This is recommended as a first corrective step when you feel your PO is unhelpful or uninterested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the IC organizational structure (Branch → Division → IC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches contain ~2–5 POs and a Branch Chief; branches are collected into Divisions; Division directors may function like Branch Chiefs and report to the IC Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize yourself with the target IC’s Organization page to identify who to contact, understand roles/responsibilities (who oversees what), and to choose an appropriate escalation path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact the Branch Chief as the first escalation step
rubrics_metrics.description: “If your PO is not your Branch Chief, that is probably your first stop.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the Branch Chief to discuss concerns about assignment or PO responsiveness — often they are directly responsible for grants in that branch and may address assignment issues or provide advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach higher-ups seeking advice, not lodging complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: When you take it up the chain, be in a stance of seeking advice rather than complaining about your rights; use language like ‘I don’t understand…there is a lack of [feedback, enthusiasm, explanation]…perhaps my applications are being assigned to the wrong PO, would another one be better?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame contacts as information-seeking and curious, not accusatory. Present uncertainty and ask whether reassignment or a different fit might be possible; this is more likely to elicit constructive help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be judicious about contacting Division Directors or IC Directors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Division directors are allowed to talk to God... they are the ones called upon in Council meetings...they are involved.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division Directors can influence funding/pickups and are a higher-level escalation point, but contacting them is situation-dependent (often influenced by your professional status and relationships). Use this route sparingly and strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize internal PO politics and shared views within a Branch
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole Branch may actually share your assigned PO’s low opinion of your work. The Chief may be totally buddies with your assigned PO...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that Branch-level consensus or relationships may limit what a Branch Chief will do; consider whether the issue is structural or reputational before escalating, and avoid burning bridges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate relationships with multiple POs over time
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is in your best interest to meet POs, many of them, and to continue your relationship with them when opportunities arise (annual scientific meetings, for example).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly engage POs at meetings and maintain contact; broad PO relationships increase the chance that someone higher up will listen or advocate for your work later.

rubrics_metrics.name: When asking for reassignment, point to another Branch’s descriptors as justification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Express doubt that the original Branch is the right one and find some key words in the description of another Branch to suggest perhaps that is a better fit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If requesting reassignment, make a concrete, constructive argument that your science aligns better with another Branch’s stated focus—use specific wording from branch descriptions to support your case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid entitled or demanding language
rubrics_metrics.description: “Keep entitled demanding far away from your thoughts. Keep angry complains about the bias and incompetence of the PO that is frustrating you out of your mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professionalism and empathy; entitlement or aggressive accusations reduce credibility and harm future interactions with PO staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that reviewers and POs may have narrow expertise and biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweet: “Valid #NIHgrant review is determined only by the aspects of the application that I excel at and any other influence is unfair bias.” (sarcastic commentary on review biases)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that reviewers and PO opinions can reflect narrow perspectives; craft applications to communicate clearly to non-specialist reviewers and anticipate divergent expertise among reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications (first-author papers) are critical for career and grant success
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s reflection: he did not grasp how important first-author publications in grad school would be until late in his postdoc; publications often measure success for hiring and grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize authorship and a publication record during graduate and postdoctoral training if you aim for a grant-funded academic career; consider tradeoffs between a monolithic thesis and publication-driven strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff-scientist job roles vary—clarify responsibilities and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to consider: What IS a ‘staff scientist’? Is it a mere evolution of a postdoc? Is it a job to generate data for a PI or to follow instructions? Does it include supervisory responsibilities? Is permanence implied? Is grant-getting removed from the role?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before taking or designing a staff-scientist position, clarify whether it is permanent, includes supervisory duties, expectations about independent work vs PI-direction, and whether it removes the need to seek grants; these affect career trajectory and funding involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor political/administrative risks to agency funding and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that agencies (EPA, USDA, potentially NIH and NSF) were ordered to halt contracts/grants and public communications: “Basically no money moving anywhere until they can take a look.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for external political actions that may temporarily freeze grants, contracts, or communications—especially for work perceived as politically sensitive; plan contingencies and be cautious about near-term reliance on pending awards.
